pos: adv. (in due measure; according to what is right)
etymology: From Latin moderatus, kept within bounds, from moderari, to regulate, related to modus, measure. The Hebrew litsdaqah means literally according to righteousness, in right measure.
biblical_def: After calling Judah to rend their hearts and turn to the LORD, Joel announces the mercy that will follow: “Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month.” The former rain fell in autumn to soften the ground for sowing; the latter rain fell in spring to swell the grain for harvest. The Hebrew word translated moderately means in righteousness or in due measure: God gives the rain exactly as it is needed, neither drowning nor starving the land. The result is abundance, “the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil” (Joel 2:24), and God promises to restore the years that the locust had eaten. Then comes the greater promise: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh” (2:28), fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-17). God measures His gifts in wisdom, and His temporal mercies point to the spiritual outpouring of the gospel age.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MODERATELY, temperately; mildly; without violence; in a middle degree; not excessively.
webster_full: MODERATE, a. Limited in quantity; not excessive; temperate; not violent.
MODERATELY, adv. Temperately; mildly; without violence.
In a middle degree; not excessively.
Joel 2:23 says God hath given the former rain moderately.
The Hebrew means in righteousness, in due measure.
scriptures: Joe 2:23

Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month.
Joe 2:24
And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil.
Joe 2:28
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that God gives His gifts in righteous measure, and His temporal mercies point to the outpouring of the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word survives in ordinary use.

Joel teaches believers to receive rain and harvest as God's measured gifts, not as accidents of climate. The same God who sends the former and latter rain in due measure pours out His Spirit upon His church. Gratitude for daily provision should lead to rejoicing in the greater gift of the gospel.

roots_lines: Latin modus, measure; moderari, to regulate.

pos: adj. and adv. (too much; beyond due measure)
etymology: From over and much, both Old English. Paul's Greek perissoteros means more abundant, excessive.
biblical_def: In his first letter Paul had commanded the Corinthians to deliver an impenitent man unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh. The discipline did its work, and the man repented. Now Paul writes: “So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.” Discipline had a purpose, the restoration of the sinner, and when that purpose was achieved the church must not keep him at arm's length. Sorrow for sin is good, for godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10), but sorrow without the comfort of forgiveness can become despair. Paul adds that the church should “confirm your love toward him” (2:8), and warns that an unforgiving spirit gives Satan an advantage, “for we are not ignorant of his devices” (2:11). Satan works in two directions: tempting the sinner to sin, then tempting him to despair once he has repented. The faithful church disciplines the impenitent and then receives the penitent with full and public forgiveness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OVERMUCH, too much; exceeding what is necessary or proper; in too great a degree.
webster_full: OVERMUCH, a. Too much; exceeding what is necessary or proper.
OVERMUCH, adv. In too great a degree.
OVERMUCH, n. More than sufficient.
2 Corinthians 2:7 warns lest the penitent be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
The church is to forgive, comfort and confirm its love to him.
scriptures: So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
Sufficient to such a man is this punishment, which was inflicted of many.
Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him.
corruption_summary: Churches either never discipline at all, or discipline without ever restoring, leaving the penitent swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
corruption_paragraphs: Where church discipline survives, it is sometimes practised as permanent exclusion, as though a fallen member could never be fully received again. That harshness gives Satan an advantage as surely as laxity does.

Paul's pattern is clear: discipline aims at restoration. When the sinner repents, the church must forgive him, comfort him and confirm its love toward him. Godly sorrow leads to repentance; overmuch sorrow, unrelieved by forgiveness, leads to despair.

roots_lines: Old English ofer and mycel.

etymology: From un-, not, and satiable, from Latin satiare, to fill, from satis, enough. The modern form is insatiable.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 16 is the LORD's indictment of Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife. He had found her as an abandoned infant, washed her, clothed her and made her His own; but she trusted in her beauty and played the harlot. Her lovers were the nations and their gods: “Thou hast played the whore also with the Assyrians, because thou wast unsatiable; yea, thou hast played the harlot with them, and yet couldest not be satisfied.” The next verse adds that she multiplied her fornication unto Chaldea, “and yet thou wast not satisfied herewith” (16:29). Idolatry is spiritual adultery, and it can never satisfy, because the heart was made for God alone. Every substitute leaves the soul hungrier than before. Augustine expressed it in his Confessions: the heart is restless until it rests in God. Jeremiah described the same folly: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Yet the chapter ends with grace: God will establish an everlasting covenant and be pacified toward her for all that she hath done (Ezekiel 16:60-63).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INSATIABLE, that cannot be satisfied or appeased; very greedy; as, an insatiable appetite or desire.
webster_full: INSATIABLE, a. That cannot be satisfied or appeased; very greedy.
UNSATIABLE, a. The older form of insatiable; not to be satisfied.
Ezekiel 16:28 says Jerusalem played the whore with the Assyrians because she was unsatiable.
She multiplied her fornication and was still not satisfied (16:29).
Idolatry is pictured as adultery against the LORD.
scriptures: Thou hast played the whore also with the Assyrians, because thou wast unsatiable; yea, thou hast played the harlot with them, and yet couldest not be satisfied.
Thou hast moreover multiplied thy fornication in the land of Canaan unto Chaldea; and yet thou wast not satisfied herewith.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
corruption_summary: Consumer culture treats endless desire as the engine of happiness, when Scripture names the unsatiable heart as the mark of idolatry that only God can fill.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern economies depend on cultivating desire that is never satisfied: the next purchase, the next experience, the next relationship. Advertising promises fulfilment and delivers appetite. Ezekiel saw the same dynamic in Jerusalem's idolatry.

Scripture diagnoses the restless heart as one made for God and turned away from Him. No created thing can fill the void. The gospel offers the only true satisfaction: the living water that Christ gives, which becomes in the believer a well of water springing up into everlasting life (John 4:14).
roots_summary: Latin satis, enough; Ezekiel 16:28 names Jerusalem unsatiable in her idolatry.
roots_lines: Latin satis, enough; satiare, to fill.
Unsatiable is the older form of insatiable.
Ezekiel 16:28 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Jerusalem multiplied her fornication and was not satisfied (16:29).
Broken cisterns can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13).

describes Jerusalem's endless idolatry
shows that no idol can satisfy the heart

etymology: From Latin frequens, crowded, repeated, constant. Paul's Greek perissoteros means more abundantly.
biblical_def: Forced to answer false apostles who boasted of their credentials, Paul reluctantly lists his own: “Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak as a fool) I am more; in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft.” What follows is a catalogue of suffering: five times beaten with thirty-nine stripes, thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, thrice shipwrecked, in perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen and of the heathen, in weariness, hunger, cold and nakedness (2 Corinthians 11:24-27). The proof of his apostleship was not success, eloquence or impressive presence, but frequent prisons and faithful suffering for Christ. He concludes: “If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities” (11:30). This turns the world's measure of ministry upside down. The true servant of Christ bears the marks of the cross, and the Lord's answer to Paul's thorn applies to every faithful minister: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FREQUENT, often seen or done; often happening at short intervals; often repeated or occurring.
webster_full: FREQUENT, a. Often seen or done; often happening at short intervals.
Used often to practice any thing; as, he was frequent in his visits.
FREQUENT, v.t. To visit often; to resort to often or habitually.
2 Corinthians 11:23 says Paul was in prisons more frequent.
His sufferings are his credentials as a minister of Christ.
scriptures: Are they ministers of Christ? (I speak as a fool) I am more; in labours more abundant, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft.
If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Ministry is measured by platform, numbers and polish, the credentials of the false apostles, rather than by faithfulness and suffering for Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The super-apostles of Corinth have heirs in every age: ministers who commend themselves by eloquence, success and charisma, and who despise the weak and suffering. Church growth methods and celebrity platforms often measure ministry the same way.

Paul's credentials were prisons, stripes and perils. The faithful minister glories in his infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon him. Churches should judge their leaders by faithfulness to the Word and willingness to suffer for it, not by the world's measures of success.

roots_lines: Latin frequens, crowded, constant, repeated.

etymology: From Latin omittere, to let go or lay aside, from ob, away, and mittere, to send. Christ's Greek aphiemi means to leave or let go.
biblical_def: In His woes against the scribes and Pharisees, Christ exposes their misplaced zeal: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.” They tithed the smallest garden herbs with scrupulous care, while neglecting justice toward their neighbours, mercy toward the needy, and faithfulness toward God. The Lord does not say that tithing herbs was wrong; He says “these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.” The problem was the inversion of priorities, a religion of minute observance that omitted the heart of the law. Micah had summed it up long before: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Micah 6:8). Sins of omission are real sins. The servant who hid his talent did nothing wicked in his own eyes, yet was condemned (Matthew 25:26-30), and James warns, “to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin” (James 4:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OMIT, to leave, pass by or neglect; to fail or forbear to do or to use; to leave out; not to insert or mention.
webster_full: OMIT, v.t. To leave, pass by or neglect; to fail or forbear to do or to use.
To leave out; not to insert or mention.
OMITTED, pp. Neglected; not done; left out.
Matthew 23:23 condemns the Pharisees for omitting the weightier matters of the law.
Judgment, mercy and faith are named as the weightier matters.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Jas 4:17
Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.
corruption_summary: Religion is reduced either to scrupulous externals that omit justice, mercy and faith, or, in reaction, to a social programme that omits the law and the gospel; Christ requires both without inversion.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pharisaic error recurs wherever religion becomes a matter of external precision while the heart remains unchanged. Its modern mirror image is the social gospel, which seizes on justice and mercy but omits faith, the law of God and the atoning work of Christ.

Christ's words cut both ways: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Faithful obedience keeps the whole law in its proper order, with the weightier matters first, and recognizes that sins of omission are as real as sins of commission.

pos: v.t. (to filter a liquid through a cloth)
etymology: From Old French estreindre, to bind tightly or squeeze, from Latin stringere, to draw tight. Christ's Greek diulizo means to filter thoroughly. The phrase strain at means to strain out.
biblical_def: Immediately after rebuking the Pharisees for tithing herbs while neglecting judgment, mercy and faith, the Lord gives one of His most memorable images: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.” The gnat was the smallest unclean creature, and a scrupulous Jew would pour his wine through a cloth to avoid swallowing one (Leviticus 11:41-43). The camel was the largest unclean animal in Palestine. The picture is deliberately absurd: the man carefully filters out the tiny gnat and then gulps down a whole camel without noticing. So the Pharisees took infinite pains over trifles while committing enormous sins of injustice, greed and hypocrisy. The Lord calls them blind guides, because they led others into the same distorted religion. The lesson is perennial. A conscience that is tender over small matters and seared over great ones is not a holy conscience but a blind one. True holiness keeps the proportions of the law, putting first what God puts first, and does not use scrupulosity over little things as a cover for neglecting the great.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STRAIN, to squeeze through a cloth or something porous for purification; to filter; to make tight; to stretch.
webster_full: STRAIN, v.t. To squeeze through a cloth or something porous for separating the liquid from the solid matter; to filter.
To stretch; to draw with force; to extend with great effort.
To put to the utmost strength; to press; to constrain.
Matthew 23:24 rebukes the Pharisees who strain at a gnat and swallow a camel.
To strain at is to strain out by filtering.
scriptures: Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
And every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth shall be an abomination; it shall not be eaten.
corruption_summary: The proverb is used to excuse all moral carefulness as legalism, when Christ condemns not care over small things but blindness to great ones.
corruption_paragraphs: Some use this verse to dismiss any concern with detailed obedience as Pharisaic gnat-straining. Christ does not condemn straining the gnat; He condemns swallowing the camel. In the previous verse He says the herbs should be tithed and the weightier matters not left undone.

The error to avoid is disproportion: a religion that obsesses over external minutiae while ignoring justice, mercy and faith, or that exalts traditions above the commandments of God. Faithful obedience attends to all God's Word in its proper order.

roots_lines: Latin stringere, to draw tight or bind.

etymology: From over and pass, from Old French passer, from Latin passus, a step. The Hebrew means to pass over or transgress beyond.
biblical_def: Jeremiah exposes the wicked men found among the LORD's people, who set traps for men and fill their houses with deceit: “They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge.” They exceeded even the wicked in their wickedness, and their chief sin was injustice toward the helpless. The fatherless and the needy had no advocate, and the very men who should have judged their cause grew rich instead. God's answer is a solemn question repeated in the chapter: “Shall I not visit for these things? saith the LORD: shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?” (Jeremiah 5:29). Throughout Scripture the LORD reveals Himself as “A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” (Psalm 68:5). Prosperity built on the neglect of the helpless is not a sign of God's favour; it is the ripening of judgment. The church, which has received mercy, is called to plead the cause of the weak.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OVERPASS, to cross; to go over; to overlook; to pass without regard; to omit; to exceed.
webster_full: OVERPASS, v.t. To cross; to go over.
To overlook; to pass without regard.
To omit in reckoning; to exceed.
Jeremiah 5:28 says the wicked overpass the deeds of the wicked.
They judged not the cause of the fatherless or the right of the needy.
scriptures: Jer 5:28
They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge.
Jer 5:29
Shall I not visit for these things? saith the LORD: shall not my soul be avenged on such a nation as this?
Psa 68:5

corruption_summary: God's concern for the fatherless is either ignored by prosperity religion or recast into secular frameworks that replace His law with ideology; Scripture grounds it in His own character as Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity preaching treats wealth as proof of God's blessing, but Jeremiah's wicked men prospered precisely while neglecting the fatherless. Their prosperity was not favour; it was the occasion of God's visitation.

Scripture grounds justice for the helpless in the character of God Himself, the Father of the fatherless and Judge of the widows. Believers plead the cause of the needy not from a secular ideology of grievance but because God commands it and will avenge the oppressed.

roots_lines: Latin passus, a step, through Old French passer.
Overpass: to go beyond, to exceed.

etymology: From Old French troubleus, from trouble, from Latin turbidus, disturbed. The Hebrew means in the strait of times, in times of distress.
biblical_def: In answer to Daniel's prayer of confession, the angel Gabriel brought the prophecy of the seventy weeks: “Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times.” The rebuilding of Jerusalem under Ezra and Nehemiah was done in troublous times indeed, with builders holding a weapon in one hand and a trowel in the other (Nehemiah 4:17). But the prophecy reaches beyond the walls to the Messiah the Prince, who “shall be cut off, but not for himself” (Daniel 9:26). Its purpose is stated in verse 24: “to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness.” Reformed interpreters have long seen this fulfilled in Christ's atoning death. The troublous times of Jerusalem's rebuilding were the prelude to the coming of the One who would build the true temple and make an end of sins.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TROUBLOUS, full of trouble or disorder; agitated; tumultuous; full of affliction.
webster_full: TROUBLOUS, a. Full of trouble or disorder; agitated; tumultuous.
Full of affliction; as, troublous times.
Daniel 9:25 says the street and wall shall be built again, even in troublous times.
The prophecy of the seventy weeks leads to Messiah the Prince.

Dan 9:24

Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.
Dan 9:26

corruption_summary: The seventy weeks are either dismissed by critics as a second-century forgery or sliced by dispensationalists into a postponed future week, both obscuring their fulfilment in Christ's atoning death.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical scholarship dates Daniel to the second century BC and treats the seventy weeks as a reinterpretation of Antiochus Epiphanes' persecution, denying genuine prophecy of the Messiah. The dictionary affirms one Daniel writing in the sixth century and a true prophecy of Christ.

Dispensationalism, for its part, detaches the seventieth week and projects it into a future tribulation, inserting a gap of two thousand years the text never mentions. Reformed interpreters read the prophecy as fulfilled in Christ, who was cut off not for Himself but to make reconciliation for iniquity and bring in everlasting righteousness.

etymology: From un-, not, corrupt, from Latin corrumpere, to destroy or spoil, and the suffix -ness. Paul's Greek adiaphthoria means incorruption or integrity.
biblical_def: Paul instructs Titus, the young pastor he left in Crete, on how to conduct himself among the churches: “In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity,” and the sentence continues, “Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you” (Titus 2:8). Uncorruptness in doctrine means teaching that is pure, unmixed with error, and not bent for gain or favour. Crete was full of “unruly and vain talkers and deceivers” who taught things they ought not “for filthy lucre's sake” (Titus 1:10-11). Against them Titus was to be a pattern: his life and his teaching must both be beyond reproach. The minister's doctrine must be uncorrupt, his manner grave, his motives sincere. This is the standard for every pastor. The church's defence against false teaching is not merely refutation but a living example of sound doctrine joined to a godly life, so that opponents are put to shame.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNCORRUPTNESS, integrity; uprightness; purity; freedom from corruption.
webster_full: UNCORRUPT, a. Not corrupt; not depraved; not perverted; pure.
UNCORRUPTNESS, n. Integrity; uprightness.
Freedom from corruption or decay.
Titus 2:7 commands Titus to show uncorruptness in doctrine.
Gravity and sincerity accompany it.

In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity,

corruption_summary: Doctrinal purity is treated as divisive rigidity, and pastors are judged by personality and influence rather than uncorrupt doctrine joined to a blameless life.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary church culture often prizes winsomeness above doctrinal integrity and treats careful theology as cold or divisive. Teachers who adjust their message for popularity or profit are tolerated as long as they are effective.

Paul requires uncorruptness in doctrine, together with gravity and sincerity. The pastor must teach what is pure, not what is profitable, and his life must give the adversary no evil thing to say. Sound doctrine and holy life together are the church's pattern.

pos: v. (past participle; opened, freed from obstruction)
etymology: From un-, reversing, and stopped, from Old English stoppian, to plug or close, from Late Latin stuppare, to stop with tow.
biblical_def: Isaiah 35 is a song of the redeemed returning to Zion. The wilderness blossoms as the rose, and God comes to save: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.” The next verse continues: “Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing” (Isaiah 35:6). When John the Baptist in prison sent to ask whether Jesus was the Coming One, the Lord answered by pointing to this very prophecy fulfilled before their eyes: “The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them” (Matthew 11:5). Christ's miracles were signs that the kingdom had come and that He was the promised Saviour. They also picture the spiritual healing He gives: by nature sinners are deaf to the voice of God, and only His sovereign word can unstop their ears. “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15). The full fulfilment awaits the resurrection, when every effect of the curse will be undone.

corruption_summary: Christ's healing miracles are either explained away by sceptics or turned by faith-healing movements into a promise of physical healing on demand, obscuring their role as signs of the King.
corruption_paragraphs: Sceptical scholarship denies the miracles or reads them as later legend. Faith-healing and word-of-faith movements, on the other side, claim that unstopped ears and opened eyes are every believer's right now, if only faith is strong enough.

Scripture presents Christ's miracles as signs authenticating Him as the promised Messiah and foreshadowing the full renewal of creation. God still heals in answer to prayer according to His will, but the miracles of the Messiah were unique credentials, and the full fulfilment of Isaiah 35 awaits the resurrection.
